systems.name: Error reporting
systems.summary: How the apps report unexpected failures from the browser, so someone looking can see what went wrong.
systems.body:
`main.tsx` calls `initTelemetry` once, as early as possible. It loads Dash0's
web SDK and starts it only when `VITE_TELEMETRY_ENDPOINT` (an OTLP/HTTP base
URL) and `VITE_TELEMETRY_TOKEN` are set, as the deploy workflow sets them.
Left unset, as they are locally, both functions do nothing and the SDK is
never fetched. If the SDK can't load, errors go unreported rather than
breaking the app. This file is the app's only tie to the vendor, so moving
off Dash0 changes it alone.

Pages call `reportError` with the error and a context of IDs and names of
things, never people's names, emails or anything they wrote. It leaves out
what the caller expects: the API's 4xx answers (not found, forbidden,
invalid), and aborted requests, which are the page moving on.

- **The token ships in the bundle**, so it must be one that can only
  ingest.
- **Only a page's origin and path are sent.** The SDK reports the page's URL
  with every error, and its query and fragment can hold a secret or what
  someone searched for, so `urlAttributeScrubber` drops them.

systems.name: Stability marks
systems.summary: How every app page shows its stability level, from one record of every feature in every app.
systems.body:
`FEATURES` in `src/featureStability.ts` names each app feature and its level,
grouped by app (`portal`, `console`, `admin`, `hub`), with the profile pages
every app has at the top. The rail (`access/navigation.ts`, drawn by
`SidebarNav`), the page header and section cards take an entry as `feature`
and show the design system's `StabilityMark` for it, so the sidebar and the
pages can't disagree, and moving a feature up is a one-line change.

- **A Prototype page is topped by `PrototypeNotice`** instead, the design
  system's `StabilityBanner`, which says plainly what isn't real on it,
  usually that it runs on the app's `data/mock.ts`. Its `PageHeader` then
  takes no `feature`, since the banner carries the level.
- **A GA feature shows no mark.** Nothing passes it a `feature`, and its
  entry stays as the record.
- **Each entry's comment is its description.** It says what the feature is,
  what's real and what isn't, and its known gaps, often only the technical
  ones where the capability doc lists the rest.
- **The levels mean what the file's header says.** Prototype runs on
  placeholder data, or changes only the page's own state. Alpha reads and
  writes the API. Beta has unit tests in CI for the logic the API doesn't
  check, reports unexpected failures (see
  [error reporting](error-reporting.md)), and has been through QA in a
  browser.

A level here is a page's, and Docket keeps levels only on capabilities. Most
pages have their capability's level. Where a page is still behind it, the
component doc says so: a client's block page in the portal, and the admin's
Scheduling, accepted agreements and engineer invitations.

components.name: Account
components.summary: The profile every app mounts at `/<app>/account`: the signed-in person's own account, their bio, their access tokens, their notification choices, and the app's theme.
components.body:
The account is the person's, not an organization's or a partnership's, so it
reads the same in every app, and its requests name no organization.

The profile (`Profile.tsx`) stands in for Clerk's `UserProfile` modal. Its
name, photo, email addresses, connected accounts, password and devices go
straight to Clerk, and reach the API through Clerk's `user.updated` webhook;
a new or removed photo also at once, as `DetailsSection` asks the API to read
it. Anything sensitive asks the person to confirm it's them first
(`ReverificationProvider`). The theme (`AppearanceSection`) is kept by this
browser, not by Clerk. It's part of no capability.

Only the profile refuses a blank name. The API accepts one, since Clerk is
the source of truth for users and takes names from sign-up, a provider or its
dashboard, and refusing its sync would leave that person unable to sign in.
For anyone without a photo, Gravatar is looked up from each viewer's
browser, by a hash of the address of whoever they're looking at, and the
page says so to people about themselves only. Unit tests in `src/account/`
cover cleaning a name, what's reported, reading Clerk's settings, how a
connected account stands, how devices are named and ordered, finding an
address already on the account, Gravatar's URL, and the token list and
limits.

The bio (`BioSection`, on the profile of someone who works with Exalynt) is
the API's, and is part of Teams, since teammates and clients read it there.
The length check is in `src/shared/bio.ts` and `src/components/BioField.tsx`,
which the admin's Teams uses too.

Access tokens and their organization limits are all the API's, read again
after each create or revoke. `tokenLimits.ts` shows only the organizations a
limited token's owner still belonged to when the page last read them, since
the API goes on returning any they've left. The example requests on the
page read the secret from the environment, so they run as they are and the
secret stays out of the shell's history.

Notifications is a Prototype on placeholder data (`data/notifications.ts`):
the choices are held in memory by `useNotificationSettings` until a reload,
Slack, Discord and Microsoft Teams are pretend, and the API sends nothing. It
shows only while the `notifications` flag is on in Flipt (`RequireFlag`).
Each app shows the notifications for who someone is in it, and in the
console, being a team lead comes from their team.

`payoutAccount/` holds the payout account page that the console and the hub
mount; it's described with them.

components.name: Admin
components.summary: The admin, where Exalynt's admins run clients, partners, engineers, teams, roles and payouts.
components.body:
The admin acts in no organization: its requests name none, so the caller's
platform role applies. It isn't gated on any agreement. Each page needs the
permissions its data takes, such as `partner:manage` for Partners or
`payout:manage` for Payouts, and the API refuses what the role doesn't allow.

Some pages are still placeholders, marked Prototype:

- The overview (`overview/`) runs on `data/mock.ts`, except its note of
  overbooked weeks (`OverbookedWeeks`), which is the API's. The API adds up
  every engineer against every booking across Exalynt, so one team's
  overbooked week can be hidden by another's spare time.
- Scheduling (`scheduling/`) runs on `data/mock.ts` and `data/teams.ts`.
  Assigning changes only the page's state. It's marked Prototype in
  `src/featureStability.ts`, below Staffing's Alpha.
- The revenue calculator (`revenue/`) runs on `data/mock.ts`. It's part of
  no capability.
- A client's Coupons tab runs on `data/coupons.ts`, held in memory until a
  reload.
- A client's Agreements tab runs on `data/agreements.ts` and
  `data/sentAgreements.ts`, over placeholder clients. It's marked Prototype,
  below Agreements' Alpha; an engineer's agreements and a partner's are real.
  `SendAgreementDialog` sends through the API only when it's given `onSend`,
  which an engineer's page passes. Without one it records the agreement in
  `data/sentAgreements.ts`, in this browser until a reload.

The rest reads and writes the API. `data/partners.ts` isn't placeholder
data: it keeps the API's partnerships in memory for the Partners pages, read
once by `loadPartners`.

Inviting people to work with Exalynt (`engineers/invitations.ts`, on the
Engineers list) is marked Alpha, below Teams' Beta, which includes it. Each
permission an invitation uses is checked apart: choosing the role takes
`role:manage`, sending it `user_role:manage`, giving it applications
`application_access:manage`, and giving it a team `team:manage`.

Each deploy of the API puts back permissions taken off Admin, Member, Billing
and Administrator, and the Roles page says so for a role by its name alone,
so a role of the other kind with one of those names says it too.

components.name: Auth
components.summary: Signing in and up, and onboarding: the pages that belong to no app, where someone gets an account and joins or creates what they'll work in.
components.body:
Sign-in and sign-up are our own forms over Clerk's `useSignIn` and
`useSignUp`. Clerk decides what each needs next, and the forms are just the
steps for each answer. A social provider leaves for its consent screen and
comes back through `/sso-callback` (`SSOCallback.tsx`). What the instance
allows, such as password length and which factors exist, is in Clerk's
dashboard, and Clerk's own error sentences are shown as they come
(`errors.ts`).

Signing in with no app asked for lands on `Landing.tsx`: someone with one app
goes straight in, someone with several picks, and someone with none goes on to
onboarding. Onboarding is where someone in no organization lands, and where an
invitation's email brings them. They accept an organization's invitation, or
an invitation to work with Exalynt, which opens the console, or go on to the
hub's welcome page for a partnership, or create an organization. Invitations
and organizations are the API's; Clerk only signs people in. Each choice
reloads the page it opens, so everything reads afresh what they've just been
given.

Sign-up, onboarding, and switching or creating organizations are GA in
`src/featureStability.ts`, with their rules covered by the API's acceptance
tests.

- **Creating an organization can't happen twice.** Onboarding holds one
  `Idempotency-Key` for it. The logo is uploaded once the organization
  exists: if that fails, the organization is kept and the page stays, to try
  the logo again or go on without it.
- **A referral code outlives the redirects.** It arrives on the sign-up link
  as `ref` and is kept in this browser (`referralCode.ts`) until the
  organization is created, past email verification or a provider's
  redirect. Where storage is unavailable, the person types it instead. A
  code the API refuses leaves nothing created.
- **Onboarding sits outside the portal's `RequireOrganization`**, which sends
  everyone in no organization there, so the redirect can't loop.

components.name: Console
components.summary: The console, where Exalynt's engineers set themselves up, claim and work their blocks, offer their time, write estimates, and see what they're paid.
components.body:
The console acts in no organization: its requests name none, so the caller's
platform role applies. Nobody works in it without an Engineer Agreement in
effect, admins who also work as engineers included. Until they've accepted
one, `Layout.tsx` puts the one sent to them in place of every page, or says
none has been sent (`ConsoleGate`). The gate is the app's alone: the API
still answers what someone's role allows without an agreement in effect, and
the admin app isn't gated at all.

Two pages are still on placeholder data from `data/mock.ts`, through
`data/relationships.ts`: the overview (`overview/`) and a client's page
(`clients/`), both topped by a `PrototypeNotice`. Neither is part of a
capability yet. The overview does read the engineer's availability and the
terms of their Engineer Agreement from the API. Everything else reads and
writes the API.

My Schedule (`assignments/`) claims and unclaims straight through the API,
which holds the staffing rules. A refusal is toasted and everything is read
again. The weekly layout is drawn like the portal's Schedule, from
`components/schedule/`.

A block's page (`blocks/`) is at the block's id, not its number, since
numbers repeat across clients; the old `/console/assignments/:id` sends on to
it. Its focus, timeline and conversations come from `src/components/block/`,
shared with the portal's block page. The timeline is Alpha and the
conversations Prototype in `src/featureStability.ts`, each with the level of
its own capability. An update's or focus's images, videos and files are
uploaded to the client's organization and read with the engineer's token
only when their section opens, and anything but a plain image or video is
only ever a download (`objectURLOf`). Until a messaging provider is set up,
conversations are kept by the noop provider and can't be opened.

The payout account page is `src/account/payoutAccount/PayoutAccountPage.tsx`,
the same page the hub mounts for a partnership, here for the engineer's own
account. It's real, through the API, on Stripe Connect.

Estimates' figures are worked out in the browser by `src/estimates/`, from
the sizes it shares with the API (`SIZES`) and the prices each estimate
carries, and unit tests pin them to the API's.

components.name: Hub
components.summary: The Partner Hub, where a partnership's manager follows the clients it has brought in, invites more, and sees what it earns and how it's paid.
components.body:
Every page acts in one of the partnerships the signed-in person manages.
`PartnershipProvider` reads them from the API and opens the one they last
looked at in this browser, or else the first by name; someone who manages
none is told the hub has nothing for them. Switching partnership gives up on
reads still going and reads everything again for the new one.

A partnership works in the hub only once its Partner Agreement is in effect:
until then `Layout.tsx` puts the agreement sent with its invitation in place
of every page, for its manager to accept, and the switcher stays. The gate is
the hub's alone: the API still answers the partnership's manager without a
Partner Agreement in effect. The welcome page (`welcome/`), where a partner
invitation lands, sits outside that gate, since someone who hasn't accepted
has no hub yet.

Every page reads and writes the API; the hub has no placeholder data.
Earnings, Payouts and Clients read every page of theirs from the API, then
page them in the browser; Home's Clients card asks for just the latest five.
The payout account page is `src/account/payoutAccount/PayoutAccountPage.tsx`,
the same page as the console's, for the partnership's own account, apart
from its manager's. `holdNotice`, which says what holds earnings up, is unit
tested.

The invitations list shows the API's refusals (an address it can't take, one
already invited, a limit reached) as the API words them. Any other failure is
worded by the page.

components.name: Portal
components.summary: The client portal, where a client organization's people buy and schedule capacity, follow their blocks, read estimates, pay, and manage the organization.
components.body:
Every page acts in the organization being looked at. `AccessProvider` holds
it and the reader's role in it, and `Layout.tsx` builds the rail from that
role: a role without capacity, estimate or team reads (Billing) doesn't get
those pages, and one without `invoice:read` (Member) doesn't get Billing. The
pages that are left check the same permissions, say why when the role can't
see them, and ask the API for nothing then. `RequireOrganization` sends
someone in no organization to onboarding, or offers someone with the console
to create one. Switching organization starts each page again.

Nobody works in an organization until its Client Agreement is in effect:
`Layout.tsx` puts the agreement in place of every page (`AgreementGate`), for
someone with `organization:manage` to accept, or tells anyone else an Admin
has to first. The organization switcher stays, to work in another. The gate
is the app's alone: the API still answers what a member's role allows
without an agreement in effect, so anything new that must wait for the
agreement has to sit behind the gate.

Every page reads and writes the API: the portal has no placeholder data
(`data/relationships.ts` only orders the API's teams). A block's own page
(`capacity/View.tsx`) is marked Prototype in `src/featureStability.ts`, below
Fulfillment's Alpha, because whether it's the right page for a client is
still the question, not because its data is fake. Its focus, timeline and
conversations are the console's, from `src/components/block/`.

The setup bubble's steps are worked out by `beforeWorkStarts`
(`components/setup/`), which unit tests cover. Estimates' figures are worked
out in the browser by `src/estimates/`, from the sizes it shares with the API
and the prices each estimate carries; unit tests pin them to the API's.

Buying holds one `Idempotency-Key` for each opening of
`PurchaseCapacityDialog`, so trying again while the dialog is open can't
charge twice, and closing it starts a new purchase with a new key. The
provider's page for an invoice is opened at an address the API reads from the
provider each time, since those addresses expire, so the portal never keeps
one. The Schedule's weeks are the API's, rolling over at midnight UTC.

gaps.text: `POST /users/me/sync` has no end-to-end test, as the API's end-to-end server runs without Clerk. Acceptance and unit tests cover it instead.
A name or primary address reaches the API only by Clerk's webhook, or by `api sync users`, so others see the old one until it arrives, and a retried older webhook can bring an old one back.
If Clerk fails to load, `ResetFailedClerk` clears Clerk's cookies and reloads, in the hope that helps, so even a brief Clerk outage signs that browser out.
Nobody has yet completed a Google connection or disconnected one, as that needs a real Google account.
Access tokens reads every page of someone's tokens, then searches, filters, sorts and pages them in the browser.

No partner has been through Access tokens in a browser, and no real screen reader has been through it or its organization limits, though it's the same page for everyone. QA only saw the limits disabled, for admins, engineers and team leads, who belong to no organization.
The Clients pages read every client and every block before showing anything, and the list pages them in the browser. Each block's invoice is read from the payment provider by the API, one at a time.
Client coupons (`data/coupons.ts`) and the revenue calculator's coupons are the same shape but separate code, and the two don't meet.
The API sends every partnership and every pending invitation at once, and the Partners and Invitations lists page them in the browser.
Each Engineers page reads everyone, every team, client and block, once when it opens and again after a team change.

The Engineers pages are written for administrators: without `user:read`, `team:read`, `capacity:read` or `client:read` the roster doesn't load, and with a team or own scope it shows only what that reaches.
The team picker on the Engineers pages shows without `team:manage`, so the change is only refused by the API, and toasted.
The Commercial Terms an admin chooses from, on an invitation or when sending an engineer new terms, come from the UI's own copy of the catalog (`src/shared/terms.ts`), not the API's.

A client's accepted agreements open their PDF from the API's agreement preview, filled in from the placeholder record each time, so they open only where `AGREEMENT_PREVIEW_ENABLED` is on (Compose, never production). They have to read the API's own agreement endpoints, as an engineer's page does.

Whether someone is ready for client work is read for one person at a time (`engineers/useReadiness.ts`), since asking whether they can be paid asks the payout provider, so the Engineers list can't show it. The list has no Agreement column either, as that would take a request per engineer.
A partner's page reads its manager's own payout account, not the partnership's.
Scheduling shows its own placeholder teams (`data/teams.ts`), which don't match the API's teams on the Teams page, so its preference for a client's teams isn't real.
Only the Roles page stops the role given to an organization's creator being unmarked or deleted. The API allows it, and the next deploy gives creators a role again.
The role editor gives a permission one scope, though the API allows several, and saving keeps only the widest, so own and team becomes team.
Roles is tested end to end only by the API's tests. The pages have no automated tests of their own.
The setup bubble reads again on each page and each time it opens, four requests and a call to the payout provider each time, until everything on it is done.
Who's ready for client work is worked out in the browser, in the console's `components/setup/` and again on the admin's engineer page, so no acceptance test covers it, and the two can drift apart.
My blocks reads every block the engineer has ever had, a page at a time.
A block's conversation counts are read when its page opens, and again when a conversation window closes, and at no other time.
Teams is tested end to end only by the API's feature tests. The console's own unit tests cover finding the engineer's team.
Changing a run of weeks takes several calls, so a failure partway leaves some weeks changed and others not. The page says it failed and shows what's there.
Earnings loads the whole list at once, with no pagination, and the API works out what's upcoming afresh on every read.
A failure to load Earnings is shown on the page but not reported to telemetry.

"This week" on My blocks and Availability is the browser's, while the API counts weeks from Monday in UTC, so around midnight on a Sunday a block can show Ready that can't be started yet, and a change to the week ending can be refused.
Saving an estimate sends the whole of it, with no check of what changed since it was opened, so of two people editing at once the last save wins.
The estimate editor is tested end to end only by the API's feature tests. The console's own tests cover the math and what a save sends.

Accepting an invitation on the welcome page is three calls: accepting, naming the partnership, and accepting its Partner Agreement. If naming fails the partner is told to name it in the hub, and if the agreement fails the hub opens on it to accept.

Earnings' screens are tested end to end only by the API's tests. The hub's unit tests cover the totals, each earning's state and note (`earningTotals`, `earningState`, `earningNote`) and reading every page.
Payouts' screens are tested end to end only by the API's tests. The hub's unit tests cover the rows (`toRows`, `failureText`) and reading every page.

Home's workflow is tested end to end only by the API's tests. The portal's own unit tests cover what the page works out (`homeState`) and what it reads (`listCurrentCapacities`), not its screens or how a section fails.
Home can't be switched off on its own, so a bad release of it is rolled back with everything else.
The setup bubble reads the blocks on now, the teams and billing when the organization changes and each time it opens, so on Home the blocks are read twice.
Each page that shows the organization's teams reads them again.
Your teams is tested end to end only by the API's feature tests. The portal's own unit tests cover reading every page of teams and the order people show in.
Capacity and the Schedule load every block the organization has bought, reading each page of them in turn, and Capacity filters, sorts and pages them in the browser.
A block's page reads every one of the organization's blocks to find this one by its number.
Billing and payment methods are tested end to end only by the API's feature tests, which run without a real payment provider.
The Members table reads every member of the organization at once, unpaged.

The portal's own unit tests on Members cover only how pasted addresses are read, what is left to retry after some invitations fail, and the role an invitation starts on. The rules are tested by the API's acceptance tests, and nothing tests the page itself.
An organization's logo is read with the session token, once per change and per page load, so the browser doesn't cache it.

tradeoffs.text: Only errors are collected: uncaught ones, and those pages pass to `reportError`. No page views, request timings or session recordings.
tradeoffs.cost: A slow page, or one people give up on without an error, leaves nothing to look at.

tradeoffs.text: Each page's level is declared once in the UI, in `src/featureStability.ts`, for the rail and the pages to read, apart from the capability docs' levels in the API's repository.
tradeoffs.cost: A level change is made in both repositories, and nothing checks that they agree.

tradeoffs.text: The session tasks Clerk can hold a session back for, a password reset it forces or two-step setup, use Clerk's own screens, dressed by `clerkAppearance`, since they're rare.
tradeoffs.cost: Those few screens look like Clerk's rather than ours.

tradeoffs.text: Payment methods, invoices and company details stay on the payment provider's own pages, which Billing opens at an address the API asks the provider for. The portal knows nothing of the provider, and shows only a label for the default payment method.
tradeoffs.cost: Clients leave the portal to see an invoice or change how they pay, and a page left open in another tab doesn't see what they changed there.

tradeoffs.text: Members show their own photo or their initials, never a Gravatar, which would send their address, hashed, to a third party.
tradeoffs.cost: A member who hasn't uploaded a photo shows initials here, though their profile shows their Gravatar.

qualities.name: Utility
qualities.question: Is it worth building, and is this the right way to build it?
qualities.why: It's worth building, and this is the right way to build it.

levels.summary: Just enough for someone to judge the idea.

outcomes.text: Those judging the idea can try it, or watch it run, enough to tell whether it's worth doing and whether this is the way to do it.

implementation.text: The question it's meant to answer written down before it's built, and the answer once it's judged.
A clickable UI with fake or hard-coded data.
Two or three versions of the key screen, to choose between.
A stub endpoint or command that returns realistic output, or a mock server from a draft API description.
One run by hand on a recent day's records, with its output shown next to the source.
A draft of the main calls and the config format, tried by one team that would use it, in a branch of their code.
A script or notebook that runs the core idea on made-up or sample data.
A spike against the one real integration the idea depends on, when that's the open question.
A dry run, a sandbox, or a test account when trying it would otherwise change a real system or reach real people.

overengineering.text: Polishing anything the idea doesn't depend on.
Building out the parts of the system that aren't the question.
Packaging an installed app when a script on sample files answers the question.
A production-like environment, infrastructure as code, or a deploy pipeline, when a local run or one preview lets people try it.
Sending real emails or texts when the question is the workflow, and showing the message on screen would answer it.
Putting it on a schedule, when running it by hand answers the question.
Building for several platforms, such as both iOS and Android, when one answers the question.

levels.summary: Real use on the real system, to learn what it should become.

outcomes.text: It works end to end on the real system.

implementation.text: Wired to real storage and services, with sample data where real data isn't needed.
Installed the way its users will get it, from a packaged build or the real registry, not run from source.

outcomes.text: It's used for real.

implementation.text: A few people, teams, or systems using it for real work, or a job running on a real schedule.
A pilot with one client or team doing real work, with their usual way of working kept as a fallback.
Run alongside what it replaces, on real input, with the results compared before anything acts on them, when a wrong result would cost money or reach customers.
Each consuming service keeps its old calculation and chooses between the two, so it can go back without a release.
Whether it's being used, and how, is known, such as from its logs or by asking those using it.

overengineering.text: Usage tracking built into what people install.

outcomes.text: What's learned from using it shapes what comes next.

implementation.text: Notes on what worked and what didn't, feeding the next round of changes.

overengineering.text: Settling its shape. Big changes are still expected.

levels.summary: Confidence that the need is real and the approach is right. From here, it's refinement.

outcomes.text: The need and the solution are confirmed, so what changes from here is refinement.

implementation.text: Feedback is about details, not direction.
Those integrating have run their real flows through it without needing a change to its shape.

outcomes.text: What success looks like is agreed.

implementation.text: Success measures agreed with whoever asked for it, such as adoption, time saved, error rates, or jobs completed.
Today's numbers measured before it's widely used, such as the current no-show rate, so there's something to compare with.
Use measured from the services it calls, such as requests by its version, not from people's devices.

overengineering.text: Analytics built into what people install, when asking them or counting what it produces would do.

levels.summary: Proof, from real use, that it delivers what it's for.

outcomes.text: It's shown to deliver what it's for in real use.

implementation.text: When it's too early to show, such as for a yearly workflow, a known gap with the date it will be shown by.
Usage or outcome numbers that meet the measures agreed at Beta.
The systems it was built for rely on it, and the copies of the logic it replaced are retired.

overengineering.text: An analytics pipeline built only to prove value, when the numbers can come from its own data or the client's reports.

qualities.name: Usability
qualities.question: Can its users learn and use it on their own?
qualities.why: Its users, people or programs, can learn it, use it, and recover from mistakes on their own.

implementation.text: Whoever built it walks those trying it through it.
Shown on the device those judging it will really use, such as a front-desk tablet or a phone.
A request collection or a few curl commands for the main calls.

overengineering.text: User docs, or polishing flows beyond what trying the idea needs.
Layouts for every screen size, when those judging it use one device.
Shell completions, colored output, spinners, and interactive prompts.
An SDK, a developer portal, generated reference docs, or self-serve sign-up.

levels.summary: The main path makes sense without the builder explaining it.

outcomes.text: Those trying it can use its main path without help from whoever built it.

implementation.text: A short note for those trying it, covering what it does, how to reach it, and what's missing.
Clear labels and an obvious flow through the main screens.
Example requests for the main endpoints, and a sample of each event it sends.
`--help` text, and a quick start from installing it to the first real run, including how to set credentials.
A README with a quick start.
A note for those reading its output: what each table or file holds, how often it's refreshed, and what's missing.

overengineering.text: Complete docs, accessibility audits.
Translations, theming, or layouts for devices those trying it don't use.
A developer portal, SDKs, or generated client libraries.
A data catalog, or a full dictionary of every column.

levels.summary: People can use all of it on their own, mistakes included.

outcomes.text: Its users can learn and use it on their own.

implementation.text: In-app help, or a guide to the main tasks.
A reference for every endpoint, such as from an OpenAPI spec, and a sandbox or test keys to try every call without real effects.
`--help` for every command, and a README.
A reference for its config file: every key, its type, its default, and an example.
Reference docs for its public API, with types and doc comments editors can show.
Its inputs, outputs, schedule, and what to do when it fails, with each output table and column described where its readers look.
A few real users watched trying the main tasks, and what tripped them up fixed.

overengineering.text: A hosted docs site, interactive tutorial, or setup wizard, when `--help`, a README, and generated reference cover it.
A self-serve portal for callers to manage keys or replay webhooks.

outcomes.text: Its users can tell what happened after everything they do, and what to do next.

implementation.text: Loading, empty, and error states handled on purpose.
Feedback for every action, showing that it's in progress, done, or failed.
Forms that validate as you go, and say what to fix.
Each item shows whether it's only on the device, waiting to sync, synced, or failed, and why.
After an import, a summary of what was read, what was skipped, and why.
Consistent status codes, and error bodies that say what went wrong without exposing internals.
Clear error messages, distinct exit codes, output that scripts can parse, and what a long step produced, such as a URL, printed at the end.
Errors with a stable code and a message naming the input that was wrong.
Those reading its output can tell when it last ran, and whether that run was complete.

outcomes.text: Its users can recover from mistakes.

implementation.text: Confirmation, undo, or a dry run before anything destructive.
A confirmation before anything destructive, skipped with `--yes` in scripts.
A way to cancel or correct what a call created.
A run can be repeated for a chosen day or batch, and replaces what that run wrote instead of adding to it.

outcomes.text: It works for everyone it's meant for.

implementation.text: Keyboard access, labels, and contrast.
Layouts that work at the screen sizes it's used on.
Usable where it's really used, such as in bright light, with gloves, or with one hand.
Runs without a terminal: no prompts, spinners, or color when output isn't one, and every prompt answerable with a flag or environment variable.
Dates, times, numbers, and languages shown the way its users expect.
Units, currencies, and time zones explicit, such as a currency code with each amount.

overengineering.text: A formal accessibility audit.
Translations into languages its users haven't asked for.

levels.summary: Polished and consistent everywhere, for everyone it's meant for.

outcomes.text: Everything it does can be learned without asking anyone.

implementation.text: Complete docs, updated with each release.
How to install, upgrade, and troubleshoot it.
A guide to running it in CI.
Docs for every webhook: its events, payloads, how to check its signature, and how retries work.
A description of every table and column it writes, with units, time zone, and how fresh the data is.
How well people complete the main tasks is measured, such as success rates or time taken.

overengineering.text: Docs for internals its users never touch.
In-app analytics to measure how people complete tasks, where watching a few people or the records they submit would do.
SDKs in several languages, when callers can work from the reference with any HTTP client.

outcomes.text: It behaves consistently across its whole interface.

implementation.text: A shared design system, so screens look and behave the same way.
Each platform's own conventions, such as back navigation, menus, shortcuts, and file dialogs.
Naming, paging, and errors consistent across every endpoint.
The same flag names and output styles across every command, such as `--json` and `--yes` meaning the same everywhere.
Names, argument order, units, and error types consistent across every export.
Table and column names, units, time zones, and what null means kept the same across every table it writes.

overengineering.text: A design system of its own, when an established component library already gives it consistency.
Screens made identical on iOS and Android against each platform's conventions.

outcomes.text: All of it works for everyone it's meant for.

implementation.text: Meets WCAG 2.2 AA, or the standard the project has adopted.
Works with VoiceOver and TalkBack, and at the largest text sizes the platform offers.
Plain output when it isn't writing to a terminal or `NO_COLOR` is set, with nothing conveyed by color alone.
For software without screens, its docs meet the accessibility standard the project uses.
Emails it sends have a plain-text version, and read well with screen readers.

overengineering.text: WCAG AAA throughout, or a formal third-party audit, unless the client or a law requires it.

qualities.name: Functionality
qualities.question: Does it do what it should, and keep doing it?
qualities.why: It does what it should, and is shown to keep doing it as it changes.

implementation.text: Run the main path by hand after each change.
A few sample inputs and their expected results in a test file, when that's quicker than checking by hand.
A handful of output rows checked against the source by hand.

overengineering.text: Automated tests, unless they're the quickest way to try the idea, or the security baseline needs one, such as a test that tenants stay apart.
Handling edge cases or bad input, unless they're the question.
Contract tests, or an API description checked on every change, before its shape has settled.

levels.summary: The main path is checked, so a change can't quietly break it.

outcomes.text: The main path is known to work after every change.

implementation.text: End-to-end tests of the main path's happy path, through the public interface, with real dependencies.
A request to each endpoint gets the response it should, and each webhook it sends arrives with the right payload.
The main flow, driven through the UI.
The main flow done offline and then synced, when working offline is part of what it's for.
Run each command on a fixture, and check its output and exit code.
Run it on sample input, and check what it wrote.
The common flows a consumer follows, through its public API.
A test that installs the packaged build or packed package the way people will, and runs its main flow.
Expected results worked out by whoever owns the rules, not copied from what the code returns.
Providers that send messages or charge money run in their test mode, or replaced by a fake, so a test run reaches no one.
Tests that change a real system run against a sandbox or test account on it, and clean up after.
Acceptance tests for the core rules it follows, each marked with the rule it verifies.
With no sandbox or test environment, a fake built from the API's docs, checked on every change, plus one real run against a test record before each release.
Tests run on every change, and a failure blocks merging.

overengineering.text: Unit and integration tests for edge cases, coverage targets, load tests.
A test for every input or combination, instead of the common ones.
A full copy of a system it reads from to test against, when a few made-up records in its format will do.
UI tests across a device farm or many OS versions.

outcomes.text: Errors are visible, never silent.

implementation.text: Input validated where it enters.
Records or files it can't process rejected with the reason, or counted and logged, never dropped quietly or partly imported without saying so.
A failed call to an outside service, such as a message that didn't send, recorded where someone can see it.
A run that fails ends as a failure the scheduler can see, never a success with nothing written.
Every failure ends with a non-zero exit code, including one reported by a service it called.
Failures return an error status, never a 200 with the error inside.
Bad input or config throws a clear error, never returns NaN, zero, or a default.
A sync that fails says so on the device, and what failed stays queued instead of looking sent.

levels.summary: Edge cases and errors are handled, and checked too.

outcomes.text: Unusual input and error paths are handled correctly.

implementation.text: Data validated before it's written.
Empty, missing, duplicate, and oversized input handled.
A repeated request or redelivered message doesn't do its work twice, such as with an idempotency key or a duplicate check, when doing it twice would create a second record or send a second message.
Two people changing the same thing at once can't both succeed unnoticed, such as with a unique constraint or a version check, where that would double-book or overwrite someone's work.
Numbers kept exact where exactness matters, such as money in integer minor units or a decimal type.
A rule for when the same item changes on the device and elsewhere before it syncs, and the person told when their change didn't win.
Records that fail validation set aside with the reason, and records changed at the source after loading updated, not added again.
Events it sends carry a unique ID and a timestamp, so receivers can drop duplicates and put them in order.
A malformed or incomplete config reported with the file, line, and key at fault, before anything is changed.

overengineering.text: Guaranteed in-order delivery of events, when each carries a timestamp or version receivers can order by.
A general sync engine or conflict-free data types, where one simple rule for conflicts is enough.
Distributed locks against overlapping runs, when the scheduler only ever starts one.

outcomes.text: How it handles unusual input and errors is known to keep working as it changes.

implementation.text: Unit tests for logic, edge cases, and failure paths.
Integration tests against the real database or systems it uses.
Acceptance tests for its edge-case rules too.
Contract tests for interfaces others depend on.
A fixed set of inputs with their expected results, checked on every change, so any changed result is seen.
Tests against a fake or recording of each outside API, kept honest by a few runs against its sandbox.
End-to-end tests of the main flows and their error states.
Tests that drop the connection, or close the app, partway through a sync.
For output that varies from run to run, such as an AI feature's, quality judged against a set of examples.

overengineering.text: Concurrency and failure-injection suites, beyond a test for each known conflict.
End-to-end tests for each edge case, where a unit or integration test checks it faster.
Tests for every combination of flags.
Running every consumer's test suite before each release.

levels.summary: Everything critical is checked on every change.

outcomes.text: Every critical workflow is known to work after every change.

implementation.text: The critical workflows agreed with the client, usually those whose failure would stop their work, lose data, or cost money.
End-to-end tests for every critical workflow.
A table of real-world cases and their expected results, checked by someone who knows the rules, and run on every change.
Anything that depends on the date or time tested across time zones and daylight-saving changes.
Contract tests against a sandbox or recording of each service it calls, plus a scheduled check against the real one.
Critical workflows tested on the packaged build, installed the way people install it.
Property-based tests where inputs vary widely.
No flaky or skipped tests left untracked.

overengineering.text: A coverage target, or end-to-end tests of every path instead of the critical ones.

outcomes.text: A fixed bug stays fixed.

implementation.text: A regression test with each bug fix.
A made-up input that reproduces each bug, never the file or record someone sent.

qualities.name: Reliability
qualities.question: Does it keep working when something goes wrong?
qualities.why: It keeps working, and recovers when something goes wrong.

implementation.text: Made-up, hard-coded, or in-memory data, local files of made-up data, or a throwaway database.
Those trying it with real work keep their usual way of recording it, so nothing real exists only in the prototype.
A local database deleted and recreated when its schema changes, with those trying it told their data won't survive a new build.

overengineering.text: Migrations, backups, retries, failover.
Resuming or undoing an operation that fails partway.
Offline sync with conflict resolution, background sync, and retry queues, unless syncing is the question.
A delivery queue, dead-letter handling, or delivery guarantees, when sending once is enough to see it work.

implementation.text: Real storage, with data that may be reset, and those using it told before a reset when it holds their real work.
A managed database's default backups left on when it holds real work, since they cost nothing to keep.
A simple forward migration, rather than a reset, when people still act on the records.
A script to reset or seed its data.
Before a build changes how data is stored on the device, work not yet sent is sent or carried over, and data it can't read is set aside, not deleted.
Output it can rebuild by running again from the source, so a reset loses nothing, and a time limit on each run so one that hangs shows as failed.
Files it writes into people's repos never overwrite their edits without asking.

overengineering.text: Down migrations, restore drills, rollback plans.
Failing over to a second provider.
Dead-letter queues and retry policies, when a failed message can be seen in the logs and resent by hand.
Background sync, resumable uploads, and retry schedules, where syncing when it opens works for those trying it.
Repair tools or automatic backups for data kept on the device.

levels.summary: Enough that people's data is safe and a bad release can be undone.

outcomes.text: Data that people or systems put in is kept across changes.

implementation.text: Versioned migrations run by the release, never by hand.
A down migration, or a backup taken before a risky change.
Automated backups, such as a managed database's defaults, even before a restore has been tested.
Queued and scheduled work, such as tomorrow's reminders, kept across deploys and restarts.
Output that can be rebuilt from its source counts as kept while the source still has it. History only it holds is backed up.
Local data migrated on upgrade, from a copy taken first and kept until the new version has opened it.
Work captured on the device kept where the OS won't clear it until the server confirms it has it, and safe to send again.
Where its local data is kept documented, so people's own backups include it.
Config files people wrote for it, and files it wrote, still work after an upgrade.

overengineering.text: Restore drills.
Snapshots of every run's output kept just in case.
A cloud backup or sync service for data on devices, when people's own backups cover where it's kept.
Versioned config schemas with automatic migration, when older config simply keeps loading.

outcomes.text: A bad release can be undone.

implementation.text: A rollback to the previous release.
Migrations that add before they remove, so the previous release still runs after a rollback.
It can be switched off quickly without a release, such as with a kill switch.
A quick fixed release.
A fixed release can open data the bad release already wrote or migrated.
The previous version made the default install again, such as by moving npm's latest tag back or reverting the Homebrew formula, and the bad one deprecated.
A remote switch and a minimum-version check in the first build people rely on, since builds already out can't gain them later.
A phased or staged rollout that can be paused if crash reports climb.
Processing paused without a release, with queued work held until it resumes, and output a bad release wrote rebuilt by rerunning those runs.

overengineering.text: A remote kill switch, and a service to host it, for installed software with no backend.
Automatic rollback to the previous version on people's devices.
Over-the-air code updates to get around store review.

outcomes.text: When something it depends on is slow or down, it fails clearly or degrades gracefully instead of hanging.

implementation.text: Timeouts on every call to a dependency, with retries only where they're safe.
A message or call that can't go through retried later or marked failed where someone will see it, never dropped.
Messages to others' systems, such as webhooks, retried with backoff when the receiver is down, and given up on after a set time with the failure recorded.
A run that can't finish leaves the last complete output in place, or marks its own as incomplete.
A clear message and a non-zero exit when a service it calls is down or too slow, so a CI job fails instead of hanging.
An unreachable update server or service never blocks the work people can do without it.

overengineering.text: Chaos testing, or running in several regions.
A transactional outbox or worker service for webhooks, when sending after the write and logging failures is enough.
A second provider to fail over to, before the first one's outages are shown to matter.
A message broker or separate queue service, when a table in its own database is enough.
Timeouts, retries, or fallbacks inside a library that calls nothing, or whose caller already retries.
Making screens work offline that aren't used offline.

levels.summary: Enough to depend on: it rides out failures, and recovery is proven.

outcomes.text: It holds up under overlapping runs, partial failures, and retries.

implementation.text: Operations safe to repeat, such as with idempotency keys or upserts.
Tests for two runs at once, and for retrying after a crash halfway through.
It fails safe where failing could cause harm, stopping rather than charging twice, sending twice, or acting on bad data.
A write that takes several steps done in one transaction, so a crash halfway leaves nothing half saved.
Rerunning any time range rebuilds what it produced, a run that starts while another is going waits or exits, and it stops when the source's data no longer has the shape it expects.
Deliveries to endpoints others run retried for a set time, then set aside for replay, so one receiver's outage doesn't hold up the rest.
Sync picks up where it left off after the app is killed or the connection drops, with IDs made on the device so a retry isn't new work.
Cancelling it, or the CI job running it, leaves nothing half-done, or a rerun finishes the job.

overengineering.text: Exactly-once delivery, where safe retries and duplicate checks are enough.
A workflow orchestrator or distributed lock service for one job on one schedule, where the scheduler's no-overlap setting or a database lock is enough.
Retries, locking, or idempotency handling in pure functions that do no I/O.
A general-purpose sync engine or CRDTs, where one person owns each record and a simple rule settles conflicts.

outcomes.text: It meets its availability target.

implementation.text: An agreed availability target, such as 99.9%, that's measured.
Its data ready by an agreed time, and queued work handled within an agreed time.
A target that fits when it's used, such as the hours its users work, and that allows for what it depends on.
Usually not applicable on people's own devices: what matters is that its main work keeps going when the services it calls are down.
Usually not applicable: the software using it holds the target.

overengineering.text: Running in several regions, or failover, beyond what the agreed target needs.
A round-the-clock target, or more nines, for work used only in business hours.
A target higher than what it depends on can deliver.
An availability target for software that runs on people's own devices.
Offline support for parts its users only use when connected.

outcomes.text: Recovering from a bad release or a loss of data is known to work.

implementation.text: A rollback that's been practiced, including upgrading, downgrading, and upgrading again.
A staged rollout that can be paused, and a minimum supported version raised with notice, after work not yet sent has finished sending.
A bad version deprecated and the previous one made the default again, tried once before it's needed.
Automated backups, with a restore that's been tested.
How much data a loss could cost, and how long recovery may take, agreed and shown in a restore test.
Output it can rebuild restored by rerunning from the source, with how far back the source keeps data known.
A copy of the local data taken before each migration, with a tested way to put it back.
For data kept only on people's devices, recovery through their own backups, shown once by copying the data folder to a fresh machine and opening it.
How much unsent work a lost device could cost is stated, and kept small by sending work as soon as there's a connection.
Migrations tried on data the size of production, made up where real data can't be copied.

overengineering.text: Tooling to restore a single tenant or record before anyone has needed it, when restoring to a copy and fixing by hand would do.
Backups and restore drills for output it can rebuild from a source that still has the data.
Backups and restore drills for software that keeps no data.
Downgrade migrations for every release of software that updates itself, where an older version can refuse newer data instead.

qualities.name: Efficiency
qualities.question: Is it fast enough, at a cost that makes sense?
qualities.why: It's fast enough for the work, at the load it gets, at a cost that makes sense.

implementation.text: Fast enough that those trying it can judge the idea.

overengineering.text: Optimizing, caching, load testing.
Caching a dependency's responses before its speed, cost, or limits get in the way of trying the idea.
Incremental loads or change capture, when a full pull of a sample answers the question.
Server-side rendering, code splitting, or a CDN for something a few people open.
Bundling into a single binary, or trimming startup time.

implementation.text: Fix what's slow enough to get in the way of real use.
Reads from systems others rely on kept light, such as off-hours, in pages, or from a replica.
Photos and large files resized before they're stored or sent.

overengineering.text: Load tests, caches, scaling work.
Incremental loads, parallel workers, or a distributed engine, when one process and a full reload finish in time.
A message queue or worker fleet, when a scheduled task handles today's volume.
Rate limits and quotas for each caller while only invited ones use it.
Memoizing, benchmarking, or bundle-size budgets before anyone has found it slow or large.

levels.summary: Fine at realistic volumes, with no runaway work.

outcomes.text: It works at realistic volumes.

implementation.text: Tried with realistic amounts of data and use.
Finishes well within its schedule at realistic volumes.
Starts quickly.
Long work, such as importing a large file, runs off the main thread with progress shown.
Tried on the oldest supported device and a slow connection, with a day's work captured offline and then synced.

overengineering.text: Performance targets, capacity planning.
Caches, read replicas, or a search engine before a real query is shown to be slow.
Incremental loads or change data capture when a full reload finishes well within its window.
Rewriting it, or bundling it into a native binary, to shave startup time nobody has noticed.
Delta updates, or shrinking the download, before its size is a problem.

outcomes.text: The work it does is bounded.

implementation.text: No query or call for each item in a list, and indexes where queries need them.
Paging, input size limits, and streaming instead of loading everything into memory.
Limits on what it accepts and returns are documented.
A cap on what it can send or spend, such as texts per hour, so a bug or abuse can't flood people or run up a bill.
Retries capped and spaced out, with work that keeps failing set aside instead of retried forever.
A limit on retries and concurrent deliveries to each receiver, so one slow one can't hold up the rest.
Reads from a source in pages or batches, within the rate limits it sets.

overengineering.text: Autoscaling workers ahead of a measured backlog.

levels.summary: Targets for speed and cost are set, and met with room to spare.

outcomes.text: It meets agreed speed targets at peak load, with headroom.

implementation.text: Measured targets for response time, throughput, or how long a job takes.
A load test at expected peak, with room to spare.
A run on the busiest day's volume, such as a seasonal peak, finishing with time to spare before its data is due.
Page load targets measured from real users' browsers, such as Core Web Vitals.
Benchmarks of the slow parts, on the devices or data sizes it's used with.
A startup-time budget for the common commands, checked in CI.

overengineering.text: Tighter targets than those agreed.
Real-user monitoring for a tool a known few people use on known machines.
Load tests of software that runs on one person's device.
Load tests of every endpoint, instead of the busiest and the critical ones.
Parallelizing or scaling out a run that already finishes well before its data is due.

outcomes.text: What it costs to run is known and acceptable.

implementation.text: What it costs per unit of work is known.
Fees charged per use by what it depends on, such as per message sent, counted in its cost, with an alert on unusual spend.
Memory, battery, and data use fit the devices it runs on.
The load it puts on the services it calls, such as calls per command and how often it polls, is known.

overengineering.text: Cutting costs beyond what's agreed to be acceptable.
Cost tracked per tenant or customer, when nobody bills or decides by it.
Tracking running costs for code that runs inside other teams' services.

outcomes.text: Its limits are known.

implementation.text: The rate limits and quotas of what it depends on fit peak use.
Alerts before it reaches a known capacity limit.
The largest tenant's or customer's data and traffic, not just the average, within what's been tested.
The largest amounts, precision, and input sizes it handles exactly, documented and tested at those limits.
Retries that back off with jitter, so many devices reconnecting at once don't swamp the service they call.

qualities.name: Security
qualities.question: Is it protected, and does it follow the rules?
qualities.why: Systems and data are protected the same way at every level, and it follows the rules that apply to it.

levels.summary: The baseline, which holds at every level: secrets and real data stay safe.

outcomes.text: Secrets stay out of code, version control, sample data, logs, and output.

implementation.text: Secrets in the environment or a secret store where it runs, with separate credentials for each environment and providers' test keys everywhere but production.
Nothing secret built into what's shipped to people's devices or published, build-time settings included.
A key that has to ship in the app, such as a maps key, treated as public and restricted to the app and the APIs it calls.
Each person's own token, kept in the OS keychain or a file only they can read, never in committed config, and redacted from debug output and errors.
Tokens read from a prompt, a file, or an environment variable, never a command-line flag, so they stay out of shell history and logs. In CI, from the CI's secret store.
Authorization headers, API keys, and tokens left out of request logs and error reports, for calls it receives and calls it makes.
API keys it issues stored hashed, and shown once.
Signing keys, store credentials, and publish tokens kept in CI's secret store, never in the repository or the project's `.npmrc`.
Only the files meant to be published go into the package, such as with a files allowlist, so no `.env` or `.npmrc` ships.
At first, the token read only from an environment variable, so the tool stores nothing and needs no sign-in.
Generated or scaffolded files refer to secrets by name, never contain their values.

overengineering.text: Keychain integration on every OS, when a file only the person can read keeps the token safe.

outcomes.text: Real data comes only through the real systems, never copied into code or fixtures.

implementation.text: Sample data that's made up, not exported from production.
Made-up names, phone numbers, and email addresses that can't belong to anyone, such as `example.com` addresses.
Made-up files in the formats it reads, with the structure of a real one and none of its values.
When a real file or record shows a problem, a made-up one that reproduces it goes into the tests, never the real one.
Recorded responses from a real service scrubbed of real names, IDs, and tokens before they're committed.
Public reference data, such as published tax rates or postal codes, used as is. A client's own records aren't.
Real data kept out of notebooks, spreadsheets, chat, and local copies outside the systems approved for it.

outcomes.text: Only those allowed can reach real systems or data, and one tenant or account never sees or changes another's.

implementation.text: Every read and write scoped to the tenant or account making it.
A test, run on every change, that one tenant can't read or change another's records, even by guessing an ID.
Work that uses real credentials isn't open to anyone who finds it, such as by running locally, on a private preview, or behind a shared password, even when its own data is made up.
Real data encrypted in transit, and at rest where it's stored, such as with HTTPS and a managed database's default encryption.
Sign-in on everything that reaches real data, with the tenant taken from the session on the server, never from what the browser sends.
Each API key tied to one caller, with the caller taken from the key, never from the request.
Webhooks and other messages carry only the receiving tenant's data, and go only to addresses that tenant registered.
Callbacks from providers, such as delivery receipts or payment events, checked as coming from that provider before they change real data.
Each person or pipeline uses credentials issued to it, never a shared or built-in one, sent only to the hosts they belong to.
The host a token is sent to comes from the tool's settings or a flag, never from a config file in a repo someone cloned.
With no sign-in of its own, data kept in the OS user's own profile, where only they can read it, on a device with disk encryption.
Where it has a sign-in of its own, data on the device belongs to the signed-in person, and work not yet sent is kept for them, not shown to the next person, when they sign out.
Its own read-only account on each system it only reads, made for the work and easy to revoke, and separate storage and output for each client it works for.
No state kept between calls that could carry one caller's data to another.
Published only by CI or named people, to the registry it's meant for, so it can't go public by mistake.
Where a client's system offers only a shared key, a test account until it issues credentials for each person or pipeline, before real data flows.
Copies it writes where others read them, such as warehouse tables, readable only by the people and roles allowed to see that data at its source.
A leaked API key stopped by disabling its record, until callers can rotate their own.
Established libraries for authentication and cryptography, never hand-rolled ones.

overengineering.text: Sign-in or tenant separation for work that holds only made-up data and reaches no real system.
Roles and permissions beyond what keeping real data apart needs, unless the client's rules call for them.
A separate database or deployment for each tenant, when scoping every query keeps them apart and no client requires more.
A sign-in of its own, or encrypting local data, on a device the OS account and disk encryption already protect, unless the client's rules call for it.
Certificate pinning, jailbreak or root detection, or app attestation, unless the client's rules call for them.
Key scopes, scheduled rotation, or self-serve key management before anyone relies on it.

outcomes.text: Personal data is collected only where it's needed.

implementation.text: Only the fields the work needs, with nothing kept just in case.
Functions and APIs take only what they need, such as a postal code instead of a whole customer record.
Personal data kept out of logs, error reports, crash reports, and analytics.
Error messages and debug output name what's wrong without repeating the personal data passed in.
Emails, texts, notifications, and webhooks carry no more personal data than they need.
Third-party services sent only what they need to do their part.
Copies it makes, such as reporting tables or exports, carry only the fields their readers need.
Location and other metadata removed from photos and files, unless the work needs them.
Device permissions, such as the camera or location, asked for only when a feature needs them.
The legal duties that come with it, such as consent, or an agreement with a provider that processes it, in place before the first real personal data arrives.

outcomes.text: Untrusted input can't run as code or commands.

implementation.text: Parameterized queries, escaped output, and no shell commands built from input.
Data from other systems treated as untrusted, even the client's own, and escaped when put into emails, messages, or pages.
Addresses callers give it, such as webhook URLs, checked so they can't reach internal systems or cloud metadata.
Sort and filter parameters matched against a list of allowed fields, never pasted into a query.
No raw HTML rendered from input.
Config and rule files parsed as data, never evaluated as code.

outcomes.text: Known problems are visible to those depending on it.

implementation.text: Known issues listed in the docs, the release notes, or its known gaps.

levels.summary: Long-term ownership, with clear ways to get help.

outcomes.text: The owner is responsible for it long term.

implementation.text: On-call, or someone to reach outside working hours, if it's critical enough.
Where failures outside working hours can wait, a check at the start of each day and a way to catch up, instead of on-call.
Reviews of serious incidents, so they're less likely to happen again.
Dependencies, runtime, and database kept on supported versions, and upgraded before their end of life.
Time planned for keeping up with each year's OS release and the stores' requirements, and for renewing signing certificates.
A support policy saying which versions get fixes, and for how long.

overengineering.text: Round-the-clock on-call for work nobody needs outside working hours.
Out-of-hours on-call for a nightly job whose output isn't read until morning, when a morning check and a rerun are enough.
On-call for a library, when its problems reach the team through its consumers during working hours.

outcomes.text: Those depending on it know where to get help, and what response to expect.

implementation.text: A support channel, with expected response times.
When it serves a client's own customers, which questions go to the client and which reach the team is clear.
A status page or announcement during an outage.
A notice to those who read its output when data is late or incomplete, and again when it's fixed.
A way to reach support from inside it, with the version and the diagnostics people choose to share.
A named contact at each team or system that integrates with it, so notices reach a person.

overengineering.text: A status page for software that keeps working when its services are down, or whose outages whoever runs those services announces.
A self-serve developer portal with sign-up and ticketing, for a handful of callers onboarded by hand.

outcomes.text: Someone other than the author can change and operate it.

implementation.text: More than one engineer able to work on it.
Where one engineer works alone, a handover note and shared access, so someone else could take over.
Building, signing, and publishing done by CI, with certificates, store accounts, and publish rights held by the client or team, not one person.
